question: How does community health nursing mainly differ from taking care of patients at the bedside?

options.A: It focuses on the health needs of a whole population
options.B: It focuses on the personal career goals of the nurse
options.C: It diagnoses just one single patient at a time
options.D: It manages the financial budget of the hospital

explanation: You've got this! While bedside nursing cares for one person at a time, community nursing looks at the big picture to help entire neighborhoods and groups stay healthy. [learn more](GNS225_U2_T19#GNS225_U2_T19_h1)

question: Why should community health nurses plan health programs *with* the people rather than just *for* them?

options.A: It guarantees that government funding will double instantly
options.B: It completely removes the need to write nursing reports
options.C: It ensures programs respect local culture and gain community support
options.D: It allows the nurse to skip doing fieldwork entirely

explanation: Great thinking! When community members are involved from the start, they trust the process more and the program actually fits their daily lives. [learn more](GNS225_U2_T19#GNS225_U2_T19_h1)

question: What is always the very first step in the community health planning cycle?
explanation: Spot on! Before you can help or build a program, you first need to assess and understand what is going on in the community. [learn more](GNS225_U2_T19#GNS225_U2_T19_h2)

question: Why is the community health planning cycle a continuous loop instead of a straight line?

options.A: Nurses must repeat the exact same paperwork every single month
options.B: Evaluation findings feed back into new assessments to improve future care
options.C: Health problems never change once an intervention is finished
options.D: It stops the community from ever joining in on healthcare

explanation: Exactly! Healthcare doesn't stop. What you learn from evaluating a project helps you plan even better care for the next round. [learn more](GNS225_U2_T19#GNS225_U2_T19_h2)

question: Which method involves a nurse driving or walking through an area to observe living conditions firsthand?
explanation: Well done! Think of a windshield survey like taking a mental snapshot through a car window—you are out there observing housing, roads, and everyday life. [learn more](GNS225_U2_T19#GNS225_U2_T19_h3)

question: A nurse only checks clinic records to decide what health program to build. What is the biggest downside to this?

options.A: It is too expensive for hospital computers
options.B: It stops doctors from writing prescriptions
options.C: It takes too many years to gather basic stats
options.D: It misses vulnerable people who never make it to the clinic

explanation: You got it! Clinic records only show those who could reach the facility. You might completely miss sick people who are too far away or can't afford transport. [learn more](GNS225_U2_T19#GNS225_U2_T19_h3)

question: When prioritizing health issues in a community, what does 'magnitude' mean?

options.A: The distance from the village to the nearest hospital
options.B: The number of people affected by the health problem
options.C: The total financial cost of medical treatment
options.D: The physical size of the local health clinic

explanation: Exactly right! Magnitude simply tells you how widespread the issue is—how many community members are actually dealing with it. [learn more](GNS225_U2_T19#GNS225_U2_T19_h4)

question: Why might a nurse rush to handle a sudden disease outbreak over a common chronic illness?

options.A: The high severity and community panic demand immediate action
options.B: Outbreaks require no financial resources or planning
options.C: Government rules forbid treating long-term conditions
options.D: Chronic illnesses are impossible to treat in communities

explanation: Spot on! Sudden outbreaks spread fast and put lives in immediate danger, so they jump straight to the top of the priority list. [learn more](GNS225_U2_T19#GNS225_U2_T19_h4)

question: What is the main reason for setting clear, measurable goals in a health plan?

options.A: To give nursing students extra homework assignments
options.B: To prevent community members from asking questions
options.C: To fulfill a strict rule just so salaries get paid
options.D: To know exactly what change is expected and when it should happen

explanation: That's correct! Clear goals give everyone a clear target and a timeline so you can easily tell if your program is working. [learn more](GNS225_U2_T19#GNS225_U2_T19_h5)

question: Which of these is a great example of a well-written community health goal?

options.A: To teach nurses how to write better charts during night shifts
options.B: To reduce childhood malnutrition in Ward 4 by 20% within six months
options.C: To talk about malaria prevention whenever people visit the clinic
options.D: To make sure everybody in the whole country feels much healthier this year

explanation: Brilliant! This goal is specific, tells you where it's happening, gives a clear percentage, and sets a realistic timeframe. [learn more](GNS225_U2_T19#GNS225_U2_T19_h5)

question: What does 'resource mobilisation' mainly mean in community health nursing?

options.A: Hiring expensive foreign experts to run local clinics
options.B: Waiting for international organizations to send free cash
options.C: Closing down rural health centers to save money
options.D: Identifying and gathering available local and outside resources

explanation: You nailed it! Resource mobilisation is all about pulling together the people, materials, and funds needed to make the health plan happen. [learn more](GNS225_U2_T19#GNS225_U2_T19_h6)

question: Why is it best to look for local strengths in the community before asking for outside donations?

options.A: External organizations refuse to work with community nurses
options.B: Local materials are always completely free of charge
options.C: Outside donors are legally banned from helping health clinics
options.D: It builds self-reliance so the program can keep running long-term

explanation: Spot on! Using local assets empowers the community so the project doesn't collapse the moment outside help stops. [learn more](GNS225_U2_T19#GNS225_U2_T19_h6)

question: When does monitoring of a community health program actually happen?

options.A: Before any assessment or planning begins
options.B: Only after the entire project has completely ended
options.C: Five years after everyone has forgotten the project
options.D: While the program is actively running

explanation: Great job! Monitoring is ongoing supervision that happens live during implementation so you can catch and fix mistakes right away. [learn more](GNS225_U2_T19#GNS225_U2_T19_h7)

question: What is the key difference between process evaluation and outcome evaluation?

options.A: Process happens before planning, while outcome happens during assessment
options.B: Process is done by doctors, while outcome is done strictly by patients
options.C: Process looks at activities done, while outcome looks at the final results achieved
options.D: Process measures money spent, while outcome measures the weather

explanation: You got it! Process check-ins ask 'Did we do the activities we planned?' while outcome checks ask 'Did health actually improve?' [learn more](GNS225_U2_T19#GNS225_U2_T19_h7)
